assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Use L1 to encode f(s) as an iterated Volterra integral. For a single local move that flips the first sign of an equal adjacent pair, isolate the changed two-step block inside the operator word. L2 shows that the inner word applied to 1 and the adjoint outer word applied to 1 are both strictly positive on (0,1). L3 shows that replacing ++ by +- or -- by -+ makes the middle block pointwise larger on (0,1). L4 transfers the outer word to the other side of the integral pairing, so the difference of the two counts is the integral of a product of two strictly positive functions; hence the count strictly increases at every allowed local move. L5 gives a finite right-to-left chain of such local moves from any sign sequence to the alternating sequence with the same last sign. Therefore every nonalternating pattern is strictly dominated by an alternating one. Finally, L6 shows that negating every sign leaves f unchanged, so the two alternating sequences have equal count. Therefore the maximizers are exactly the alternating sign sequences.

steps.derives: Fix n >= 2 and an arbitrary sign sequence s of length n - 1. Apply L5 with m = n - 1. Obtain an alternating sequence t of length n - 1, characterized by t_{n-1} = s_{n-1} and t_i t_{i+1} = -1 for all 1 <= i <= n - 2, together with a chain u^(0),u^(1),...,u^(r) such that u^(0)=s, u^(r)=t, and each transition u^(k) -> u^(k+1) flips exactly one entry j_k for which u^(k)_{j_k} = u^(k)_{j_k+1}. If s is not alternating, then r >= 1.
steps.trivial_justification: This step uses the explicit combinatorial construction in L5 to produce both the alternating endpoint and the full chain of local moves.

steps.derives: Fix one transition u^(k) -> u^(k+1) from A1, and let j_k be its changed index. Define V_k to be the operator word T_{u^(k)_{j_k-1}} o ... o T_{u^(k)_1}, with V_k = Id when j_k = 1, and define U_k to be the operator word T_{u^(k)_{n-1}} o ... o T_{u^(k)_{j_k+2}}, with U_k = Id when j_k = n - 2. Because only the sign at position j_k changes and because u^(k)_{j_k} = u^(k)_{j_k+1}, L1 gives the two formulas f(u^(k)) / n! = int_0^1 (U_k(B_k(V_k 1)))(x) dx and f(u^(k+1)) / n! = int_0^1 (U_k(B'_k(V_k 1)))(x) dx, where in the case u^(k)_{j_k} = u^(k)_{j_k+1} = +1 one has B_k = T_+ o T_+ and B'_k = T_+ o T_-, and in the case u^(k)_{j_k} = u^(k)_{j_k+1} = -1 one has B_k = T_- o T_- and B'_k = T_- o T_+.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the operator-word decomposition at the modified index furnished by L1; it isolates the unchanged outer words U_k and V_k and the two-step middle block that differs between the two sign sequences.

steps.derives: For the same k, let g_k = V_k 1 and let h_k = U_k^* 1, where U_k^* is the reversed sign-swapped word from L4. By L2, both g_k and h_k are continuous, nonnegative on [0,1], and strictly positive on (0,1). This remains true when U_k or V_k is the empty word, because L2 includes the empty-word case and then the resulting function is the constant 1.
steps.trivial_justification: L2 applies directly to the two finite words V_k and U_k^*; the positivity conclusions are needed on both sides of the later pairing.

steps.derives: Define d_k = (B'_k - B_k) g_k. In the ++ case, d_k = T_+(T_- g_k) - T_+(T_+ g_k); in the -- case, d_k = T_-(T_+ g_k) - T_-(T_- g_k). Since g_k is strictly positive on (0,1) by A3, L3 gives d_k(x) > 0 for every x in (0,1).
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the strict pointwise comparison from L3, applied to the positive function g_k produced in A3.

steps.derives: From A2, f(u^(k+1)) - f(u^(k)) = n! * int_0^1 (U_k d_k)(x) dx. Apply L4 with u = d_k, v = 1, and operator word U = U_k to rewrite this as n! * int_0^1 d_k(x) h_k(x) dx, where h_k = U_k^* 1 is the positive function from A3. Because both d_k and h_k are strictly positive on (0,1), their product has strictly positive integral over [0,1]. Therefore f(u^(k+1)) > f(u^(k)).
steps.trivial_justification: The adjoint identity from L4 transfers U_k to the other side of the pairing, and the positivity information from A3-A4 then makes the resulting integral strictly positive.

steps.derives: If s is not alternating, then A1 gives r >= 1. Applying A5 successively to each of the r local moves in the chain yields f(u^(1)) > f(u^(0)), f(u^(2)) > f(u^(1)), ..., f(u^(r)) > f(u^(r-1)). By transitivity, f(t) = f(u^(r)) > f(u^(0)) = f(s). Hence every nonalternating sign sequence has strictly smaller count than some alternating sign sequence and therefore cannot be a maximizer.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a finite induction along the chain produced in A1, using the strict increase from A5 at each link.

steps.derives: Let u^+ and u^- be the two alternating sign sequences of length n - 1. They satisfy u^- = -u^+. By L6, f(u^+) = f(u^-). Denote this common value by M.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a direct application of the sign-negation symmetry in L6 to the pair of alternating sequences, which are negatives of each other.

steps.derives: If s is alternating, then s is one of the two sequences u^+ or u^- and therefore f(s) = M by A7. If s is not alternating, then A6 gives an alternating sequence t with f(s) < f(t), and A7 shows f(t) = M. Hence f(s) is maximal exactly when s is alternating, equivalently exactly when s_i s_{i+1} = -1 for every 1 <= i <= n - 2. This is precisely the characterization of the maximizing sequences required in the theorem.
steps.trivial_justification: A6 rules out every nonalternating pattern, while A7 identifies the common maximal value attained by the two alternating patterns.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Define E_n to be the count of the alternating sign pattern starting with +, and use sign-negation symmetry to note that the alternating pattern starting with - has the same count. Prove by strong induction on n that every sign pattern of length n-1 has count at most E_n, with equality exactly for alternating patterns. For the induction step, fix an arbitrary sign sequence s and decompose F_n(s) by the position of the minimum element 1. The admissible positions are exactly the valley positions of s, and each choice of valley position j contributes a binomial factor times the counts of the left and right subpatterns. By the induction hypothesis, those smaller counts are bounded by E_{j-1} and E_{n-j}, so F_n(s) is bounded by a weighted sum over the valley set V(s). The valley set is always sparse, meaning it has no consecutive positions. The bottleneck lemma L5 says that among all sparse subsets of {1,...,n}, the maximum of this weighted sum is E_n, and equality occurs only for the odd or even parity subsets. Therefore F_n(s) <= E_n for every s, and if equality holds then the valley set must be a parity class. The valley-set characterization from L2 then forces s itself to be alternating. Conversely, the two alternating sign sequences have count E_n by definition and sign-negation symmetry. Hence the maximizing sign sequences are exactly the alternating ones.

steps.derives: Define E_0 = 1 and E_1 = 1, and for every integer m >= 2 let E_m be the number of permutations of {1,...,m} whose adjacent inequalities alternate <,>,<,>,.... By L4, for every m >= 2 the numbers E_m satisfy the two parity convolution identities E_m = sum over odd j of binomial(m-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{m-j} and also E_m = sum over even j of the same weights. By L3, if altPlus_m is the alternating sign sequence +1,-1,+1,-1,... of length m-1 and altMinus_m = -altPlus_m, then F_m(altPlus_m) = F_m(altMinus_m) = E_m.
steps.trivial_justification: This step introduces the benchmark sequence E_m and records the two facts about it that will be used later: the parity recurrences from L4 and the equality of the two alternating sign-pattern counts from L3.

steps.derives: For each integer m >= 2, let P(m) be the assertion that every sign sequence t of length m-1 satisfies F_m(t) <= E_m, and that equality holds if and only if t is alternating. The base case P(2) is true: the only sign sequences of length 1 are (+1) and (-1), both are alternating because there is no index i with 1 <= i <= 0 to check, and each is realized by exactly one permutation of {1,2}, so both have count E_2 = 1.
steps.trivial_justification: This establishes the induction predicate and verifies the smallest nontrivial size directly.

steps.derives: Fix an integer n >= 3, assume P(m) holds for every integer m with 2 <= m < n, and let s be an arbitrary sign sequence of length n-1. Define V = Val(s). By L1, writing the theorem's count as F_n(s), one has F_n(s) = sum over j in V of binomial(n-1,j-1) * F_{j-1}(s^L_j) * F_{n-j}(s^R_j), where s^L_j and s^R_j are the left and right sign subsequences determined by the valley position j.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the exact decomposition by the position of the minimum entry 1 supplied by L1.

steps.derives: By L2, the valley set V has no two consecutive integers. Also, for each j in V, the left size j-1 and the right size n-j are both strictly smaller than n. If j-1 >= 2, the induction hypothesis P(j-1) gives F_{j-1}(s^L_j) <= E_{j-1}; if j-1 is 0 or 1, then F_{j-1}(s^L_j) = E_{j-1} by the definitions of F_0, F_1, E_0, and E_1. The same reasoning gives F_{n-j}(s^R_j) <= E_{n-j}. Therefore every summand in A3 is at most binomial(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j}, so F_n(s) <= sum over j in V of w_j, where w_j = binomial(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j}.
steps.trivial_justification: This step combines the exact recurrence from A3 with the induction bounds on all smaller left and right subproblems, and it also records that V is a sparse subset so that L5 can be applied next.

steps.derives: Because V has no two consecutive integers by A4, L5 applies to the sparse set V and the weights w_j = binomial(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j}. Hence sum over j in V of w_j <= E_n. Combining this with the inequality from A4 yields F_n(s) <= E_n.
steps.trivial_justification: A4 reduced the problem to a weighted sparse-set sum, and L5 gives the sharp universal upper bound E_n for exactly such sums.

steps.derives: Assume in addition that F_n(s) = E_n. From A4 and A5 we have F_n(s) <= sum over j in V of w_j <= E_n, so both inequalities must be equalities. Therefore sum over j in V of w_j = E_n. By the equality statement in L5, the sparse set V is either the set of odd integers in {1,...,n} or the set of even integers in {1,...,n}. Applying L2, this implies that s is alternating.
steps.trivial_justification: The equality case in L5 identifies the only valley sets that can attain the upper bound, and L2 translates those valley sets back into the corresponding alternating sign sequences.

steps.derives: Conversely, if s is alternating, then s is either altPlus_n or altMinus_n. By A1, both of these sign sequences have count E_n. Hence every alternating sign sequence satisfies F_n(s) = E_n.
steps.trivial_justification: There are exactly two alternating sign sequences of length n-1, and A1 already identified the count of each of them as E_n.

steps.derives: For the arbitrary n >= 3 fixed in the induction step, A5 shows that every sign sequence s of length n-1 satisfies F_n(s) <= E_n, A6 shows that equality implies s is alternating, and A7 shows that every alternating s attains equality. Thus P(n) holds. Since A2 established P(2), strong induction yields P(n) for every integer n >= 2.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the formal closure of the strong induction: the base case was proved in A2 and the induction step was established by A3 through A7.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Work with the extended counts F_m so that subproblems of sizes 0 and 1 are allowed. Introduce E_m as the number of alternating permutations with comparison pattern <,>,<,>.... By direct definition, altPlus_m has count E_m, and by sign-negation symmetry altMinus_m also has count E_m. Prove by strong induction on n that every sign sequence s of length n-1 satisfies F_n(s) <= E_n, with equality exactly for alternating s. For the induction step, decompose F_n(s) by the position of the minimum entry 1 using L1; the admissible positions are exactly the valley set Val(s). By L2 this valley set is sparse. Apply the induction hypothesis to the left and right subpatterns arising in each summand to bound F_n(s) by a weighted sum over Val(s), with weights w_j = binomial(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j}. Lemma L5 is the explicit bottleneck: among all sparse subsets, such a weighted sum is bounded by the larger of the odd-parity and even-parity totals. Lemma L4 evaluates both parity totals as E_n. Hence F_n(s) <= E_n. If equality holds, then the sparse-set inequality of L5 is also an equality, so Val(s) must be a parity class; L2 then forces s to be alternating. Conversely, if s is alternating, then L2 shows s is altPlus_n or altMinus_n, and the initial benchmark steps give F_n(s) = E_n. Therefore the maximizing sign sequences are exactly the alternating ones.

steps.derives: Define E_0 = 1 and E_1 = 1. For every integer m >= 2, let E_m be the number of permutations b = (b_1,...,b_m) of {1,2,...,m} satisfying b_1 < b_2 > b_3 < b_4 > ... with alternating inequalities starting with <. Then for every integer m >= 2, F_m(altPlus_m) = E_m.
steps.trivial_justification: By the definitions of F_m, altPlus_m, and E_m, both sides count exactly the same permutations: those whose adjacent comparisons are <, >, <, >, ... .

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2, F_m(altMinus_m) = E_m.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix m >= 2. The sequence altMinus_m is the entrywise negation of altPlus_m. Applying L3 with n = m and s = altPlus_m gives F_m(altMinus_m) = F_m(altPlus_m). Step A1 identifies F_m(altPlus_m) with E_m, so F_m(altMinus_m) = E_m.

steps.trivial_justification: The only sign sequences of length 1 are altPlus_2 and altMinus_2. Both are alternating because there is no index i with 1 <= i <= 0 to check. By A1 and A2, both have count E_2. Hence every length-1 sign pattern satisfies the desired bound, and equality holds exactly for the alternating patterns.

steps.derives: Fix an integer n >= 3, and assume P(m) holds for every integer m with 2 <= m < n. Let s = (s_1,...,s_{n-1}) be any sign sequence with entries in {+1,-1}. Define V = Val(s). For each j in V, define s^L_j to be (s_1,...,s_{j-2}) if j >= 2 and the empty sequence if j = 1, and define s^R_j to be (s_{j+1},...,s_{n-1}) if j <= n - 1 and the empty sequence if j = n. Then F_n(s) = sum over j in V of binomial(n - 1, j - 1) * F_{j-1}(s^L_j) * F_{n-j}(s^R_j).
steps.trivial_justification: This is the exact decomposition from L1, obtained by partitioning the counted permutations according to the position of the minimum value 1.

steps.derives: With n, s, V, s^L_j, and s^R_j as in A5, the set V has no two consecutive integers. Also, for each j in V, both sizes j - 1 and n - j are strictly smaller than n. If j - 1 >= 2, the induction hypothesis P(j - 1) gives F_{j-1}(s^L_j) <= E_{j-1}; if j - 1 is 0 or 1, then F_{j-1}(s^L_j) = E_{j-1} by the definitions F_0(empty) = 1, F_1(empty) = 1, E_0 = 1, and E_1 = 1. The same reasoning gives F_{n-j}(s^R_j) <= E_{n-j}. Therefore, for every j in V, binomial(n - 1, j - 1) * F_{j-1}(s^L_j) * F_{n-j}(s^R_j) <= w_j, where w_j = binomial(n - 1, j - 1) * E_{j-1} * E_{n-j}. Summing the termwise inequalities in the recurrence of A5 yields F_n(s) <= sum over j in V of w_j.
steps.trivial_justification: L2 gives the sparsity of V. The induction hypothesis bounds every nontrivial left or right subproblem, while the size-0 and size-1 cases are handled directly from the definitions. Since all factors are nonnegative counts, the bounds multiply termwise and then sum over j in V.

steps.derives: Because V has no two consecutive integers by A6, L5 applies to V and the weights w_j. Hence sum over j in V of w_j is at most max( sum over odd j with 1 <= j <= n of w_j, sum over even j with 1 <= j <= n of w_j ). Step A3 identifies both parity sums with E_n. Therefore sum over j in V of w_j <= E_n, and combining this with A6 gives F_n(s) <= E_n.
steps.trivial_justification: A6 reduces the permutation problem to a weighted sparse-subset sum. L5 bounds that sparse-set sum by the larger parity-class total, and A3 evaluates each parity-class total as E_n.

steps.derives: Assume in addition that F_n(s) = E_n. Step A6 gives F_n(s) <= sum over j in V of w_j, and step A7 gives sum over j in V of w_j <= E_n. Since the leftmost and rightmost quantities are equal, both inequalities must be equalities. Thus sum over j in V of w_j = max( sum over odd j of w_j, sum over even j of w_j ). The equality clause in L5 therefore implies that V is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,n} or exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,n}.
steps.trivial_justification: The chain F_n(s) <= sum_{j in V} w_j <= E_n collapses to equality because the endpoints agree. L5 then characterizes the only sparse subsets that can attain the parity-class maximum.

steps.derives: Under the equality hypothesis F_n(s) = E_n, the sign sequence s is alternating.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A8 shows that Val(s) is one of the two parity classes. The final characterization in L2 states exactly that this happens if and only if s_i s_{i+1} = -1 for every 1 <= i <= n - 2, which is the definition of an alternating sign sequence.
